patient.chief_complaint: Severe headache yesterday, partially treated, 'I get bad headaches all the time'
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Foster is a 46-year-old woman with fibromyalgia and chronic headaches who presents 18 hours after a severe headache episode. She reports that yesterday afternoon while folding laundry she developed a headache that was sudden in onset, rated 10/10, which she initially attributed to one of her chronic headache episodes. She took two acetaminophen tablets and lay down. The headache partially improved to 6/10 overnight but has not fully resolved, which she describes as unusual - her typical chronic headaches resolve with rest and OTC analgesics within 2-4 hours. Her husband noted she was 'different' yesterday - more irritable, less responsive, and napped for 6 hours straight. She denies loss of consciousness, vomiting, or focal deficits. She admits her headache history complicates her own assessment. On exam today she is alert but has mild residual headache and mild neck stiffness that she attributes to 'fibromyalgia flare.' The treating emergency physician initially triages this as a chronic headache exacerbation but a consultant neurologist requests SAH workup given the sudden onset and atypical features.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL 3mm; EOM intact; no papilledema; no CN deficit
neurological_exam.additional: Mild nuchal rigidity - she attributes to fibromyalgia; Kernig equivocal; blood pressure elevated

additional_observations: No acute intracranial abnormality on initial review
CT performed 18 hours after onset - sensitivity has declined from peak
Subtle sulcal effacement difficult to exclude on current read
ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space. No mass, hemorrhage, or midline shift. Note: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid hemorrhage decreases substantially after 6 hours; a negative study does not exclude the diagnosis at this time point.
recommended_actions: Lumbar puncture recommended if clinical suspicion persists

ecg.interpretation: Normal sinus rhythm, rate 88. T-wave inversions V2–V4. QTc 472 ms. No ST-segment elevation. No pathological Q waves.

output.impression: 1. Irregular saccular aneurysm at the left posterior communicating artery, 4.6 x 3.8 mm. 2. No additional intracranial aneurysm. Conventional DSA recommended for definitive characterization.
recommended_actions: Conventional DSA recommended for definitive characterization

output.proposed: Nimodipine 60 mg q4h with current medications
interactions: Duloxetine + nimodipine: minimal direct interaction but monitor QTc given duloxetine QT effects
warnings: Hold cyclobenzaprine during acute SAH phase

findings.status: Mild vasospasm ipsilateral to left PComA aneurysm

output.impression: Day 4 TCD: left MCA MFV 124 cm/s, Lindegaard ratio 3.2 (mild vasospasm); right MCA MFV 96 cm/s (normal); basilar MFV 58 cm/s (normal). Findings consistent with mild left MCA vasospasm. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: Chronic headache history SAH diagnosis thunderclap presentation pitfalls

results.finding: Chronic headache history does NOT reduce risk of SAH - thunderclap onset always requires evaluation
Ottawa SAH rule does not exclude patients with prior headache history
Premature closure (assuming chronic headache) is a major diagnostic error leading to missed SAH

output.summary: Chronic headache history is one of the most dangerous red herrings in SAH diagnosis. The sudden-onset thunderclap headache superimposed on chronic headache history requires the same workup. The key distinguishing feature is the instantaneous onset, which is classic for SAH regardless of headache history.

output.impression: Normal echocardiogram. LVEF 58%. Normal wall motion. No Takotsubo pattern.
CT perfusion: left MCA territory CBF mildly reduced at 36 mL/100g/min; CBV preserved (no infarction); TTP mildly prolonged. Right hemisphere and posterior fossa within normal limits.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from left posterior communicating artery aneurysm (Hunt-Hess 2, delayed presentation)

differential.key_features: CSF xanthochromia confirms SAH; sudden onset atypical for fibromyalgia headache

differential.diagnosis: Chronic daily headache with acute exacerbation
differential.key_features: Thunderclap onset and CSF positive for SAH

optimal_actions.action: LP with spectrophotometry - despite chronic headache history
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Xanthochromia confirmed - subacute SAH 18 hours ago

optimal_actions.action: Literature search - chronic headache SAH pitfall
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic headache history is a red herring - thunderclap always requires workup

critical_actions: LP mandatory despite chronic headache history and negative CT
Do not attribute thunderclap headache to chronic headache without LP
Nimodipine urgently - day 2 approaching peak vasospasm window
Recognize fibromyalgia/chronic headache as diagnostic red herring
contraindicated_actions: Do not discharge with diagnosis of chronic headache exacerbation without SAH workup
Do not let chronic headache history cause premature diagnostic closure
Do not skip LP because CT is negative
key_reasoning_points: Fibromyalgia and chronic headache history are classic diagnostic red herrings for SAH misdiagnosis
The key feature distinguishing this from chronic headache: instantaneous thunderclap onset
CT negative at 18 hours is expected (sensitivity ~90%); LP with spectrophotometry is still required
Xanthochromia without fresh blood confirms subacute SAH from 12-24 hours prior
18-hour delay in diagnosis is common in patients with chronic headache - education is important
Husband's observation of behavioral change is an important clinical clue

red_herrings.data_point: History of fibromyalgia and chronic headaches
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lead clinician to attribute severe headache to fibromyalgia or chronic headache exacerbation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Chronic headache history does not reduce SAH risk; thunderclap onset is always an alarm sign

red_herrings.data_point: Patient attributes neck stiffness to fibromyalgia flare
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lead clinician to accept patient's attribution and not perform LP
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neck stiffness + thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise; patient self-attribution is unreliable in this context
